props.title: Rattlers

sections.content: **Rattlers (1976)** (1976) belongs to the distinctive wave of eco-horror films that emerged in the 1970s, following the massive success of Jaws (1975). Director John McCauley tapped into America's environmental anxieties with this tale of venomous snakes attacking a small desert community. While lacking the technical polish of similar films like Kingdom of the Spiders (1977) or Frogs (1972), Rattlers delivers memorable B-movie thrills through practical effects and real rattlesnakes, creating genuine tension despite its modest budget.

sections.content: The 1970s creature feature boom reflected growing environmental consciousness and distrust of military/scientific tampering with nature. **Piranha** (1978), **Day of the Animals** (1977), and **Night of the Lepus** (1972) all followed similar formulas - isolated communities, military/scientific mishaps, and nature striking back. **Rattlers** specifically plays on fears of chemical weapons testing, as its snakes are mutated by military experiments. SUBHEAD: The Snake Horror Subgenre

Snake horror films form their own distinct tradition, from **Ssssss** (1973) to **Anaconda** (1997) and **Snakes on a Plane** (2006). **Rattlers** stands out for using actual rattlesnakes rather than rubber props or CGI, creating an authentic menace missing from many later entries. While crude by modern standards, its practical effects and documentary-style snake footage influenced later films like **Venom** (1981).
